panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Apical four-chamber echocardiographic view of Case 39, a human patient with tricuspid atresia. The red arrow marks the absent right atrioventricular connection, the defining feature of tricuspid atresia; the RV is hypoplastic and the RA enlarged, with a dilated coronary sinus, all classic echo manifestations of the configured disease. B: Five-chamber apical echocardiographic view of the same tricuspid atresia patient (Case 39). The image shows the hypoplastic right ventricle and the associated common arterial trunk overriding the ventricular septum above a large outlet VSD, part of the documented tricuspid atresia anatomy in this case. C: Subcostal echocardiographic view of the same tricuspid atresia patient (Case 39) showing common arterial trunk type 1 with the outlet VSD (yellow arrow) and a hypoplastic right ventricle, consistent with the case's documented tricuspid atresia with common arterial trunk.

in_text_mentions: th absent right atrioventricular connection. The left ventricle (LV) was fully developed with a normal size mitral valve with mild regurgitation. A large CAT overrode the ventricular septum above a large outlet juxta-arterial VSD (Figure 2). From the CAT originated successively the coronary arteries, a short pulmonary arterial trunk with two normal size pulmonary arteries, and a left aortic arch. There was no arterial duct. The patient was discharged after leaving the maternity ward. Furosemide therapy was initiated at 2 weeks of age because of clinical signs of excessive pulmonary blood flow.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Transthoracic echocardiogram apical four-chamber view in a neonate (five days of life) directly demonstrating the atretic tricuspid valve and hypoplastic right ventricle, the defining features of tricuspid atresia; caption and disease-focused article title both support attribution. B: Color Doppler echocardiogram from the same neonate demonstrating flow across a large ventricular septal defect, an integral part of the tricuspid atresia single-ventricle physiology described in the caption and in-text mentions; the VSD flow itself is not in the allowed vocabulary so it is recorded as a proposed finding. C: Additional apical echocardiographic view of the same neonate emphasizing single-ventricle morphology with a rudimentary right ventricular component, consistent with tricuspid atresia physiology as stated in the caption and article title.
panels.attribution_text: Jalal et al. Successful Management of a Neonate With Tricuspid Atresia, Double Outlet Right Ventricle, and L-malposed Great Arteries.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.114675. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrating tricuspid atresia and single‑ventricle physiology. A) Apical four-chamber view showing an atretic tricuspid valve (yellow arrow) and hypoplastic right ventricle (red arrow). B) Color Doppler imaging demonstrating flow across a large ventricular septal defect (blue arrow) from the dominant left ventricle to the diminutive right ventricular outflow (pink arrow). Arrows indicate the turbulent jet across the septal defect. C) Additional apical view emphasizing single-ventricle morphology (orange arrows) and rudimentary right ventricular component (green arrows).
in_text_mentions: hocardiogram at five days of life confirmed complex single ventricle with double inlet left ventricle, right atrioventricular valve atresia, double outlet infundibular chamber with L-malposed great arteries arising from the small right outflow chamber with pulmonary hypoplasia, mild rightward malalignment of the conal septum, leading to sub-pulmonary narrowing, redundant and aneurysmal atrial septum with a moderate patent foramen ovale (PFO) and unrestrictive right to left shunt as shown in Figures 1A-1C. The ductus arteriosus was not seen on echocardiography, so it was not clipped or ligated.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Subcostal echocardiogram showing right atrioventricular valve atresia and a very hypoplastic right ventricle with enlarged left heart cavities — core diagnostic features of tricuspid atresia in a 21-year-old patient. [raw subtype: type IIB] B: Color Doppler echocardiogram showing marked mitral regurgitation into the left ventricle, a documented valvular dysfunction in this patient with type IIB tricuspid atresia. [raw subtype: type IIB] C: Subcostal echocardiogram demonstrating a large interatrial septal defect (arrow) producing an atrial-level right-to-left shunt, a hallmark of tricuspid atresia physiology. [raw subtype: type IIB] D: Long-axis echocardiogram showing the interventricular septal defect (arrow) and the pulmonary valve–LV connection, which the caption explicitly states characterizes type IIB tricuspid atresia. [raw subtype: type IIB]

RA: right atrium; LA: left atrium; PT: pulmonary trunk; RV: right ventricle; LV: left ventricle.
in_text_mentions: Echocardiogram: Absence of atrioventricular connection on the right, with ventricular-arterial discordance and extensive septal defects, both interatrial (34 mm) and interventricular (22 mm), and posterior deviation of the infundibular septum with pulmonary subvalvular stenosis. Pulmonary trunk dilatation was observed, and the mitral valve showed double dysfunction. The left ventricle (LV) was dilated, with an ejection fraction of 54%. Maximum pressure gradient LV-PT = 58 to 77 mmHg. (Figure 2).

A: Panel A is a real patient transthoracic echocardiogram explicitly captioned as tricuspid atresia with hypoplastic right ventricle, a specific manifestation of the configured target disease. B: Panel B is from the same neonatal echocardiogram in a case of ductal-dependent tricuspid atresia and shows a restrictive ventricular septal defect, an associated lesion commonly necessary in tricuspid atresia; no exact target-disease vocabulary key for VSD, so proposed finding. C: Panel C is an echocardiographic image from the same neonate with tricuspid atresia and shows severe right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, an expected associated anatomic feature; no exact vocabulary key. D: Panel D is an echocardiographic image from the same neonate with tricuspid atresia and shows a hypoplastic main pulmonary artery, an associated finding; no exact target-disease vocabulary key.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial CT four-chamber view from a patient with confirmed tricuspid atresia; caption explicitly labels tricuspid valve atresia, hypoplastic RV, large ASD, and LV enlargement/hypertrophy, all direct manifestations of the target disease. B: Axial CT showing an atretic, calcified aortic valve arising from a hypoplastic RV in a patient with tricuspid atresia and L-TGA; hypoplastic RV is a core manifestation of the target disease. C: Axial CT demonstrating hypoplastic ascending aorta anterior to the main pulmonary artery in a patient with tricuspid atresia and TGA; the great-artery anatomy is a direct manifestation of the target disease, though no vocabulary finding key applies. D: Axial CT showing dilated central pulmonary arteries indicating pulmonary hypertension, a documented manifestation in this tricuspid atresia patient (in-text: severe pulmonary hypertension); no vocabulary finding key applies.

There is a large atrial septal defect (red arrow), and the left ventricle is enlarged and hypertrophic (yellow arrowhead). (B) Atretic and calcified aortic valve (red arrow) originating from hypoplastic RV (L‐TGA). (C) Hypoplastic ascending aorta (blue arrow) located anterior to the main pulmonary artery (yellow arrow). Both coronary arteries (green arrows) have normal anatomy. (D) Dilated central pulmonary arteries (yellow arrows) indicate pulmonary hypertension.
in_text_mentions: k with a right bundle branch block (Figure 1). Echocardiography showed tricuspid atresia with transposition of the great arteries (TGA type), severe pulmonary hypertension (mean of PAP: 85 mmHg), and dominant left ventricle with LVEF: 35%. Cardiothoracic CT was done to evaluate better the cardiac structure, which revealed a large pulmonary trunk, hypoplastic ascending aorta, aortic arch with large PDA, and interrupted aorta. Detailed findings of the cardiothoracic CT scan are shown in Figures 2 and 3. In abdominal CT, an accidental finding was bilateral perirenal fluid accumulation (Figure 4).
